content: Effective moisture and microbial control is essential for the success of dental restoration procedures. The rubber dam is a widely used isolation method in restorative dentistry. However, the impact of rubber dam usage on the longevity and quality of dental restorations still requires further evidence-based evaluation. This review aimed to compare the effects of rubber dam isolation with other isolation methods in dental restorative treatments. It is an update of a Cochrane Review initially published in 2016. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of rubber dam isolation compared to other isolation techniques for both direct and indirect restorative treatments in dental patients. The search strategy involved a comprehensive review of multiple electronic databases, including Cochrane Oral Health's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and SciELO, up to January 13, 2021. Additional searches were conducted in Chinese databases such as CBM, VIP, and CNKI, as well as trial registries like ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (including split-mouth designs) lasting over one month that compared rubber dam isolation with alternative isolation methods for dental restorative treatments. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. The review adhered to Cochrane's statistical guidelines, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Six studies conducted between 2010 and 2015 were included, involving a total of 1,342 participants, though 233 participants were lost to follow-up. All studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias. Five studies compared rubber dam isolation with traditional cotton roll isolation. One study was excluded from the analysis due to inconsistencies in the data. Of the remaining four trials, three reported survival rates of restorations with a minimum follow-up of six months. Pooled data from two studies involving 192 participants suggested that rubber dam isolation may improve the survival rates of direct composite restorations in non-carious cervical lesions (NCCLs) at six months (odds ratio [OR] 2.29, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05 to 4.99; low-certainty evidence). However, at 12 months (OR 1.38, 95% CI 0.45 to 4.28; 1 study, 30 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and 18 months (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.25; 1 study, 30 participants; very low-certainty evidence), the use of rubber dam appeared to have little to no effect on restoration survival rates compared to cotton rolls. The evidence at these time points is very uncertain. At 24 months, one study involving 559 participants suggested that rubber dam usage might reduce the risk of failure in children undergoing proximal atraumatic restorative treatment in primary molars (hazard ratio [HR] 0.80, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; very low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence remains very uncertain. None of the included studies reported adverse effects or provided information on the direct costs of treatment. In conclusion, this review found low-certainty evidence that rubber dam isolation may reduce the failure rate of dental restorations compared to cotton roll isolation after six months. At other time points, the evidence is very uncertain. Further high-quality research is needed to evaluate the effects of rubber dam usage on various types of restorative treatments.
